parts.text: The LORD speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives instructions for voluntary burnt offerings. An offering from the herd must be an unblemished male. The worshiper lays a hand on its head and kills it, while Aaron’s sons handle the blood and arrange the altar fire. The animal is prepared and washed, then burned as an offering accepted to make atonement.

Similar instructions govern offerings from the flock. Those bringing birds may offer turtledoves or young pigeons, with the priest performing the prescribed preparation. Though the animals and procedures differ, each burnt offering is presented upon the altar as an offering made by fire, a sweet savor to the LORD.

chapters.title: Grain offerings and the covenant’s salt

parts.text: God describes grain (meat) offerings of fine flour, oil, and frankincense. A priest burns a memorial portion on the altar, while the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons as most holy. Offerings may also be baked in an oven, on a pan, or in a fryingpan, following instructions about flour, oil, and unleavened preparation.

No offering burned to the LORD is to contain leaven or honey, although these may be presented as firstfruits. Every offering must include salt, identified with God’s covenant. Firstfruits grain may be brought as green ears dried by fire, with oil and frankincense; its memorial portion is burned on the altar.

A peace offering from the herd may be male or female but must be without blemish. The worshiper lays a hand on its head and kills it at the tabernacle entrance. The priests sprinkle its blood around the altar and burn specified fat and organs upon the burnt offering. A lamb from the flock is presented with similar procedures, including its fat tail.

A goat may likewise be offered, with its blood handled by the priests and its designated fat burned on the altar. These instructions distinguish the portions offered to the LORD from ordinary food. The chapter concludes with a lasting rule for Israel’s generations and dwelling places: they must eat neither fat nor blood.

The LORD provides sin offerings for offenses committed through ignorance. If the anointed priest sins, he offers a bullock, with blood applied inside the sanctuary and to the incense altar. Its fat is burned on the altar, but the remainder is burned outside the camp. A bullock is also required when the whole congregation becomes guilty and later recognizes its offense; the elders lay their hands on it.

A ruler brings a male goat, while an ordinary person brings a female goat or lamb. These offerings use blood on the burnt-offering altar rather than the inner procedures prescribed for the priest and congregation. The priest makes atonement according to the specified rite, and the offender is forgiven.

The chapter identifies guilt arising from withholding testimony, contact with uncleanness, and careless oaths. Once aware of the offense, a person must confess and bring the required offering. Provision is made for poverty: someone unable to afford a lamb may bring two birds, and someone unable to afford birds may bring fine flour without oil or frankincense. The priest makes atonement, and forgiveness follows.

A person who unintentionally misuses the LORD’s holy things must bring a ram and restore the loss with an additional fifth. A ram is also prescribed for guilt incurred by violating a command even when the person did not know it. The offering acknowledges responsibility before the LORD.

chapters.title: Restitution and the priests’ handling of offerings

parts.text: Someone who deceives a neighbor about entrusted property, robbery, oppression, or a lost possession and swears falsely must restore the property and add a fifth. A ram is brought for atonement and forgiveness. Instructions then address the burnt offering: the priest removes its ashes in prescribed garments, and the altar fire must be kept burning continually.

The grain (meat) offering’s memorial portion is burned, and the priests eat the remainder unleavened in the holy place. The priests’ own consecration grain (meat) offering is burned entirely rather than eaten. Further rules govern the sin offering’s sacred flesh, garments marked by sacrificial blood, vessels used to cook the offering, and who may eat it. Offerings whose blood is brought inside the sanctuary for atonement are burned instead of eaten.

God gives further rules for trespass offerings, including their blood, fat, and the priests’ portions. Different grain (meat) offerings are distributed according to their preparation. Peace offerings of thanksgiving must be eaten the same day, while offerings connected with a vow or voluntary gift may also be eaten the next day. Flesh remaining beyond the permitted time must be burned, and uncleanness excludes a person from the sacred meal.

Israel must not eat the fat reserved for offerings or the blood of animals and birds. In peace offerings, the breast is waved before the LORD and the right shoulder is given to the officiating priest. These portions belong to Aaron and his sons. The chapter closes by gathering the offering laws given to Moses at Sinai.

chapters.title: Aaron and his sons are consecrated

parts.text: Moses assembles the congregation at the tabernacle and carries out the LORD’s instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons. He washes them, clothes Aaron in the priestly garments, and anoints the tabernacle, its furnishings, the altar, and Aaron. He clothes Aaron’s sons and offers a bullock for sin, using its blood to purify and sanctify the altar.

Moses offers a ram as a burnt offering and another for consecration. Blood touches the priests’ right ears, thumbs, and great toes, and prescribed portions are waved and burned. Oil and blood are sprinkled upon the priests and their garments. They eat the consecration meal and remain at the tabernacle entrance for seven days, doing what the LORD commanded.

chapters.title: Priestly service begins and God’s glory appears

parts.text: On the eighth day, Moses summons Aaron, his sons, and Israel’s elders. He directs offerings for Aaron and the people, announcing that the LORD will appear to them. Aaron approaches the altar and offers a sin offering and burnt offering for himself, with his sons assisting in the handling of blood and the preparation of the sacrifice.

Aaron then presents the people’s sin offering, burnt offering, grain (meat) offering, and peace offerings according to the prescribed order. He blesses the congregation. Moses and Aaron enter the tabernacle, come out, and bless the people again. The glory of the LORD appears to all, and fire comes out from before him to consume the offering on the altar. The people shout and fall on their faces.

chapters.title: Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD

parts.text: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire before the LORD, and fire from him kills them. Moses declares that God will be sanctified by those who approach him. Their bodies are carried outside the camp. Aaron and his remaining sons are warned not to abandon their priestly duties in mourning. God forbids priests to drink wine or strong drink when entering the tabernacle, so they can distinguish holy from unholy and teach Israel.

Moses explains the remaining priests’ sacred food portions. Finding the sin offering burned instead of eaten, he questions Eleazar and Ithamar. Aaron explains his concern about eating it after the day’s calamity, and Moses accepts his answer.

The LORD distinguishes creatures Israel may eat from those they must avoid. Land animals must both divide the hoof and chew the cud; water creatures must have fins and scales. Particular birds are forbidden. Most flying creeping creatures are excluded, with specified jumping insects permitted. The distinctions govern food rather than allowing Israel to choose freely among all creatures.

Contact with the carcasses of unclean animals makes people and certain objects unclean, with washing, waiting until evening, or destruction required according to the case. Additional rules address creeping creatures, vessels, water, seed, and animals that die naturally. God calls Israel to holiness because he is holy and brought them out of Egypt to be their God.

The LORD gives Moses rules for a woman’s purification after childbirth. Following the birth of a son, she is unclean for seven days, the child is circumcised on the eighth day, and her further purification lasts thirty-three days. Following a daughter’s birth, the corresponding periods are fourteen and sixty-six days. During purification she must not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary.

When the appointed days end, she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a bird for a sin offering. If she cannot afford a lamb, two birds are accepted instead. The priest makes atonement for her, and she is pronounced clean from the flow of blood.

chapters.title: Examination of skin diseases and affected garments

parts.text: God instructs the priests how to examine swellings, scabs, bright spots, boils, burns, and scalp or beard conditions. The appearance, depth, hair color, spread, and development of a condition determine whether someone is pronounced clean or unclean, sometimes after repeated periods of isolation. Ordinary baldness is not itself uncleanness. A person declared leprous must wear torn clothes, cover the upper lip, announce uncleanness, and live outside the camp.

The chapter also addresses spreading marks in wool, linen, and leather. A priest inspects and isolates affected items, then orders washing, removal of a damaged part, or burning according to how the mark develops. These procedures distinguish what can be cleansed from what must be destroyed.

For a person healed of leprosy, the priest conducts an examination outside the camp and a cleansing ceremony involving two birds, cedar wood, scarlet, hyssop, and running water. Washing, shaving, and a further waiting period follow. On the eighth day, sacrifices are brought, and blood and oil are applied in prescribed ways. Reduced offerings are allowed for a poor person, while retaining the required atonement procedures.

God also gives rules for affected houses in the land Israel will receive. A priest examines the walls after the house is emptied. Suspect houses are closed, and damaged stones and plaster may be removed. Persistent spreading contamination requires demolition. A cleansed house receives a ceremony with birds and the other specified materials. The laws distinguish clean conditions from unclean ones.

The LORD gives rules concerning a man’s bodily discharge and the uncleanness of bedding, seats, objects, and people touched by it. Washing and waiting periods are required, and after the discharge ends the man counts seven days, washes, and brings two birds for offerings on the eighth day. Separate instructions address an emission of seed and uncleanness associated with sexual intercourse.

A woman’s ordinary menstrual period brings a seven-day separation, with rules for contact with her and her bedding. An abnormal or prolonged discharge requires a further count of seven days after it stops and offerings afterward. These instructions separate Israel from uncleanness so they do not defile God’s tabernacle among them and incur death.

Following the death of Aaron’s sons, God restricts entry behind the veil. On the appointed occasion, Aaron must wash, wear linen garments, and bring offerings for himself and the people. Lots distinguish a goat for the LORD from the scapegoat. Incense covers the mercy seat, and sacrificial blood is used to make atonement for the sanctuary, tabernacle, and altar because of Israel’s uncleanness and sins.

Aaron confesses Israel’s iniquities over the living goat, which is sent into the wilderness bearing them. Washing and further offerings complete the service, while the sin-offering remains are burned outside the camp. This atonement is commanded once each year on the tenth day of the seventh month, a day of rest and afflicting their souls for all the people.

chapters.title: Sacrifice at the sanctuary and the prohibition of blood

parts.text: God requires sacrificial animals to be brought to the tabernacle entrance and offered through the priest, rather than killed as unauthorized sacrifices in the open fields. The command turns Israel away from sacrifices to devils. Both Israelites and resident strangers who offer burnt offerings or sacrifices elsewhere are to be cut off from among their people.

Eating blood is forbidden because the life of the flesh is in the blood, which God has given upon the altar to make atonement. Blood from hunted edible animals must be poured out and covered with dust. Anyone eating an animal that died naturally or was torn by beasts must wash and remain unclean until evening, bearing guilt if the cleansing is neglected.

The LORD commands Israel not to copy Egypt’s practices or those of Canaan, but to follow his statutes and judgments. He prohibits sexual relations within specified close family relationships, including parents, siblings, grandchildren, aunts, daughters-in-law, and brothers’ wives. Other prohibitions address a woman together with her daughter or granddaughter and taking a wife’s sister as a rival during the wife’s lifetime.

Further commands forbid intercourse during a woman’s separation, adultery, giving children to Molech, a man lying with a man as with a woman, and bestiality. God declares that such practices have defiled the nations and the land. Israel and the strangers among them must avoid these abominations, lest the land also cast them out.

chapters.title: Holiness in worship and everyday conduct

parts.text: God calls Israel to be holy because he is holy. Commands join reverence for parents and sabbaths with rejection of idols and proper sacrifices. Harvesters must leave gleanings for the poor and stranger. The people must not steal, lie, defraud, withhold wages, curse the deaf or put a stumblingblock before the blind, distort justice, or spread slander. Rather than harbor hatred or seek revenge, they must rebuke wrongdoing and love their neighbor as themselves.

Further statutes govern mixed kinds, sexual wrongdoing involving a bondwoman, fruit trees, blood, divination, and practices associated with the dead. Israel must honor the aged, reverence the sanctuary, reject familiar spirits, love the resident stranger, and use honest weights and measures. God repeatedly grounds these commands in his identity as the LORD.

chapters.title: Penalties for grave offenses and a call to separation

parts.text: The LORD establishes penalties for giving children to Molech, consulting familiar spirits, cursing parents, adultery, and other forbidden sexual acts. The community must not conceal Molech worship, for God will judge both the offender and those who turn a blind eye. He commands the people to sanctify themselves and keep his statutes, identifying himself as the LORD who sanctifies them.

Further laws address prohibited relationships and their consequences. Israel must not follow the customs of the nations being driven out, lest the land also reject them. God has separated Israel to belong to him and promises them a land flowing with milk and honey. They must therefore distinguish clean from unclean creatures and remain holy to him.

The priests receive particular restrictions concerning contact with the dead, mourning practices, and marriage because they offer the food of their God. Ordinary priests may mourn certain close relatives, but the high priest must not defile himself even for father or mother or abandon his consecrated position. His marriage is restricted to a virgin of his own people.

Descendants of Aaron with specified bodily blemishes may not approach the altar or pass within the veil to present offerings. They are nevertheless permitted to eat the sacred food allotted to the priestly household, both holy and most holy. These distinctions protect the sanctity of the sanctuary without removing those men from the provision made for Aaron’s family.

chapters.title: Respect for holy gifts and acceptable sacrifices

parts.text: God warns Aaron’s descendants to treat Israel’s holy offerings with reverence. Priests must not eat sacred food while unclean; washing and the appointed waiting period restore eligibility in the specified cases. Rules distinguish members of a priest’s household who may eat from outsiders who may not. Someone eating holy food unintentionally must repay its value and add a fifth.

Offerings brought to fulfill vows or as voluntary gifts must meet the required standards. Animals with serious defects are not acceptable, with a limited distinction for certain voluntary offerings. Newborn animals remain with their mothers seven days before becoming eligible, and a mother and her young must not be killed on the same day. God commands obedience and reverence for his holy name.

God sets out Israel’s sacred assemblies, beginning with the weekly sabbath. Passover is followed by seven days of unleavened bread. At harvest, the first sheaf is presented before new grain is eaten. Seven complete sabbaths are counted, and on the fiftieth day a new grain (meat) offering is brought with the prescribed sacrifices. Harvest gleanings must still be left for the poor and stranger.

The seventh month includes a memorial of blowing trumpets, the day of atonement with rest and affliction of soul, and the seven-day feast of tabernacles followed by an eighth-day assembly. During tabernacles Israel rejoices and dwells in booths, remembering how God housed their fathers after bringing them out of Egypt. Each observance has its appointed offerings and restrictions on work.

chapters.title: The lamps, shewbread, and judgment for blasphemy

parts.text: Israel must provide pure olive oil so Aaron can keep the lamps burning before the LORD from evening until morning. Twelve cakes of fine flour are arranged in two rows on the pure table, with frankincense as a memorial offering. The bread is renewed each sabbath and belongs to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place under a lasting covenant.

A man with an Israelite mother and Egyptian father blasphemes the LORD’s name during a fight. He is held until God’s judgment is declared, then taken outside the camp and stoned. The LORD gives the same rule for stranger and native, and states principles of punishment and restitution for killing or injuring people and animals. Israel carries out the command.

The land must rest every seventh year. After seven cycles of seven years, the fiftieth year is proclaimed as jubile, beginning with a trumpet on the day of atonement. Liberty is announced, and people return to their families and inherited possessions. Land transactions are valued by the harvests remaining until jubile. God promises provision for obedience and declares that the land belongs to him, with Israel living as strangers and sojourners before him.

Rules allow relatives to redeem land sold through poverty and distinguish rural property, walled-city houses, and Levitical property. Israelites must support impoverished brethren without interest and must not treat an Israelite servant harshly as a bondman. Redemption and release at jubile protect Israelites sold into service, because they are God’s servants whom he redeemed from Egypt.

chapters.title: Blessings, judgments, and remembrance of the covenant

parts.text: God forbids idols and commands reverence for his sabbaths and sanctuary. If Israel keeps his statutes, he promises rain, fruitful harvests, peace, victory, growth, and his dwelling among them. If they reject his commands and break his covenant, escalating judgments will follow: disease, defeat, failed harvests, wild beasts, war, and famine. Repeated refusal to listen brings further chastisement.

Persistent rebellion will lead to terrible hunger, ruined cities and sanctuaries, scattering among the nations, and fear in exile. The deserted land will enjoy the sabbaths Israel denied it. Yet if the people confess their sin and humble their hearts, God will remember his covenant with the patriarchs and the land. Even in their enemies’ countries, he will not utterly destroy them or forget his covenant.

The final chapter governs vows involving the valuation of persons, with assessments according to age and sex and adjustment by the priest for someone too poor to pay. Animals suitable for sacrifice become holy when vowed and cannot simply be exchanged; an attempted exchange makes both animals holy. Other animals are valued by the priest, and redemption requires an added fifth.

Rules also cover houses and fields dedicated to the LORD, with field values related to the years remaining until jubile. Certain devoted possessions cannot be redeemed, and firstborn animals already belonging to God cannot be newly dedicated by a vow. Tithes of produce and every tenth animal are holy to the LORD, with specified redemption rules and no selective exchange of livestock.
